My grandfather kept his shop at the narrow end of Fell Street, in a room so crowded with clocks that strangers entering it for the first time usually stopped in the doorway, as if they had walked in on a conversation. I had been coming there since I was seven, and to me the ticking was only the shape the silence took.

He worked at a bench beneath a green lamp, a loupe screwed into one eye, surrounded by trays of parts sorted by a system he had never written down and could not explain. Customers brought him wristwatches, carriage clocks, once a barometer, and he took each one in with the same slight nod, as though it had been expected.

On the shelf above the bench stood a mantel clock of no particular beauty, a squat walnut thing with a chipped dial, which he took down every Tuesday, opened, cleaned, and put back. It never ran more than a week. I asked him at last why he did not simply fit a new movement, since even I could see the old one was past saving.

"Because Mrs. Aveline brings it in," he said.

"She brings it in every Tuesday."

"She does."

"And you charge her nothing."

He set the loupe on the bench and looked at me with the patience he reserved for customers who wanted a repair finished by Friday. "She comes on Tuesdays," he said, "because her husband died on a Tuesday, and on Tuesdays her house is very loud." He turned the mainspring a quarter turn and listened. "The clock is not the work."

I was sixteen and had lately learned to keep my face still, so I said nothing. But I began that winter to notice how many of his repairs took longer than they needed to, and for whom.

passage:
Before the compressor, cold was not manufactured but harvested. For the first half of the nineteenth century, the ice that cooled a Charleston sickroom or a Calcutta clubhouse had been sawn in slabs from a frozen New England pond and carried south in the hold of a ship.

The trade began in 1806 as a private conviction. Frederic Tudor, a Boston merchant of twenty-two, filled a brig with ice from his family's pond and sent it to Martinique, where he expected the heat to sell it for him. The heat did not. He had no storehouse waiting at the far end, no customers who had ever handled ice, and no dependable way to keep the cargo from becoming the ocean it was floating on. He lost the money, and later, for related debts, his liberty.

What made the trade pay was never the ice, which cost nothing, but the removal of everything that wasted it. Tudor built insulated icehouses in the southern ports before he shipped, so that a cargo had somewhere to go. He gave ice away to bartenders and physicians until a city that had lived without it could not, manufacturing the demand he had once assumed was already there. And after 1825 he adopted a horse-drawn cutter devised by Nathaniel Wyeth, which scored the surface of a pond into a grid so that workers could pry up blocks of a single size. Uniform blocks stacked without gaps, and ice that touches only ice melts slowly. Packed in sawdust from the Maine sawmills, a shipment could cross the equator and arrive two-thirds whole.

By the 1850s Boston sent ice to ports on four continents. The industry ended not by being outsold but by being outgrown: the machines that made cold on demand needed no winter at all.

passage:
When Marion Held carried a folding stool to the corner of Ninth and Vine in the summer of 1961, the traffic engineers who watched from the municipal building assumed she was waiting for a bus. She was not. For eleven weeks she sat and counted: how many people crossed against the light, how long they lingered at the newsstand, which of the four benches went unused from morning until dark. Her notebooks, now held by the city archive, contain almost no opinions. They contain tallies.

This was a modest method, and its modesty was the point. Planners of that era worked chiefly from aerial photographs and projected traffic volumes, instruments that flatter the designer by showing a city as it looks from above rather than as it is used from within. Held distrusted the view from above. A plaza that photographed handsomely, she noted, might be crossed by two thousand people a day and sat in by nine, and the nine would be sitting on the low wall at its edge rather than on the benches provided at its center. Numbers of that kind were difficult to argue with, because they were not arguments. They were counts.

The findings did not make her popular. When she reported that a newly opened civic square was being used mainly as a shortcut, the department that had built it questioned her sample, and then, more quietly, her standing to comment. Held answered by expanding the sample. Over the next decade she trained ninety volunteers, who between them logged more than four thousand hours on benches, curbs, and low walls in eleven cities.

She never proposed a grand theory of urban life, and she was impatient with those who did. Asked late in her career what her research had established, she said only that most public spaces fail in ways anyone might have noticed by sitting still for an afternoon.

passage:
For most of the twentieth century, the standard account of how a forest works was an account of competition. Trees were understood as solitary organisms locked in a slow contest for light, water, and mineral nutrients, and a mature stand was read as the record of that contest: the winners standing, the losers gone. The account was not wrong so much as partial. It described what could be seen above the soil line and almost nothing of what happened below it.

Beneath a temperate forest floor lies a dense mesh of fungal filaments called hyphae, each far thinner than a root hair. Many of these fungi form partnerships with tree roots, wrapping or penetrating them in structures known as mycorrhizae. The arrangement is an exchange. Fungi cannot photosynthesize, so they draw sugars from the tree. In return, their filaments reach into pores of soil too fine for any root to enter, gathering phosphorus and nitrogen and passing them upward. A single fungus may join dozens of trees at once, and a single tree may host several fungal species, so that the mesh under a hectare of woodland is less a set of paired partnerships than a shared circuitry.

These partnerships have been known since the nineteenth century. What changed, beginning in the 1990s, was the ability to trace what moved through them. Researchers exposed one tree to carbon dioxide made with a heavy isotope of carbon, a label that could be detected later in wood and leaf. When the labelled carbon turned up weeks afterward in a neighbouring tree of a different species, leakage through the soil was a strained explanation. Further trials found that shaded seedlings, which fix little carbon of their own, received proportionally more of the label than seedlings standing in full sun.

Such results have been reported widely as evidence that trees feed one another, and the language of generosity has proved hard to resist. It should be resisted a while longer. The quantities are small, a few percent of a seedling's yearly budget in most trials, and small quantities can be moved by processes that intend nothing at all. The fungus sits between the two trees and takes a share of everything that passes. A filament keeping a shaded seedling barely alive may be protecting its own future supply rather than performing a kindness, and no experiment yet distinguishes a forest of donors from a forest of hosts being farmed by a third party.

What the work does establish is narrower and still considerable: the boundary of a tree is not where its bark ends. Carbon, water, and warning signals cross between individuals along routes that no one bothered to look for while the contest for light seemed explanation enough. Whether that traffic is charity, tax, or theft is a question the isotopes cannot answer, and one that will be settled, if at all, by patience rather than by metaphor.

passage:
For most of the last century, planners assumed that the time a city dweller spent travelling to work was a fact about the city rather than about the traveller. A cramped medieval town would produce short journeys; a sprawling suburb, long ones. When survey data from dozens of countries were finally laid side by side in the 1970s, the assumption did not survive. Whatever the era or the technology, the average daily journey came out at roughly an hour, divided between the morning and the evening. Villagers who walked, clerks who took streetcars, and engineers who drove motorways all appeared to be spending the same portion of the day in transit.

The finding has since been given a name, the travel-time budget, and, like most tidy generalizations about human behaviour, it has been asked to carry more weight than it can bear. In its modest form it claims only that populations, averaged over time, hold their daily travel near a stable figure. In the form that circulates in newspapers, it becomes a law of nature: an inner clock that dictates how far any person will go. The gap between the two is the difference between a regularity and an explanation.

What might account for the regularity is easier to guess than to demonstrate. One line of argument is economic. Faster transport does not hand commuters an hour back; it hands them a wider circle of houses to choose from, and they spend the saving on space, quiet, or a garden rather than on time. The budget, on this reading, is not a constraint the traveller obeys but the residue of a bargain the traveller strikes. A second line is biological, holding that an hour of daily movement suits us for reasons older than cities, and here the evidence thins considerably; the case rests more on its own plausibility than on measurement.

The distinction matters because policy follows from it. If the hour is a bargain, a new rail line will not empty the roads: it will lengthen the commutes of people who move further out, and the traffic will return within a decade. If the hour is a fixed appetite, the same line ought to reduce the total distance travelled. Cities have, in effect, run the experiment many times, and the roads have generally refilled. That is a point in favour of the bargain, though not a proof of it. The refilling might have other causes, and the surveys behind the original figure counted only the journeys people reported, never the ones they quietly gave up.

For most of the last century, planners assumed that the time a city dweller spent travelling to work was a fact about the city rather than about the traveller. A cramped medieval town would produce short journeys; a sprawling suburb, long ones. When survey data from dozens of countries were finally laid side by side in the 1970s, the assumption did not survive. Whatever the era or the technology, the average daily journey came out at roughly an hour, divided between the morning and the evening. Villagers who walked, clerks who took streetcars, and engineers who drove motorways all appeared to be spending the same portion of the day in transit.

The finding has since been given a name, the travel-time budget, and, like most tidy generalizations about human behaviour, it has been asked to carry more weight than it can bear. In its modest form it claims only that populations, averaged over time, hold their daily travel near a stable figure. In the form that circulates in newspapers, it becomes a law of nature: an inner clock that dictates how far any person will go. The gap between the two is the difference between a regularity and an explanation.

What might account for the regularity is easier to guess than to demonstrate. One line of argument is economic. Faster transport does not hand commuters an hour back; it hands them a wider circle of houses to choose from, and they spend the saving on space, quiet, or a garden rather than on time. The budget, on this reading, is not a constraint the traveller obeys but the residue of a bargain the traveller strikes. A second line is biological, holding that an hour of daily movement suits us for reasons older than cities, and here the evidence thins considerably; the case rests more on its own plausibility than on measurement.

The distinction matters because policy follows from it. If the hour is a bargain, a new rail line will not empty the roads: it will lengthen the commutes of people who move further out, and the traffic will return within a decade. If the hour is a fixed appetite, the same line ought to reduce the total distance travelled. Cities have, in effect, run the experiment many times, and the roads have generally refilled. That is a point in favour of the bargain, though not a proof of it. The refilling might have other causes, and the surveys behind the original figure counted only the journeys people reported, never the ones they quietly gave up.

On the train down she had assembled, out of nothing at all, a couple who kept the hedges square and lined the pantry shelves with the same paper her mother had used, and by the time the taxi turned in at the gate the invention had hardened into something she half expected to find.

What she found was a young man in a cardigan two sizes too large, holding the door open with his foot because his hands were full of a cat. He said his name was Petersen and that he had been told to expect her at four. It was ten past three. Ada apologised for the trains, which had run exactly to time, and stepped into a hall that smelled of paint and coffee and not at all of the sea.

The clock was where she had left it, on the shelf above the fireplace, though the fireplace itself had been boarded and painted over, and someone had set a row of paperbacks along the mantel where the photographs used to stand. Petersen watched her look at the books.

"We can move those," he said.

"They're yours," said Ada. "It's only the clock I've come for."

He lifted it down and held it out with both hands, the way a person holds something he has decided in advance is precious, and Ada took it and found it lighter than she remembered: a thin brass case, a face gone the colour of weak tea. For eleven years she had thought of it as the last heavy thing in the house.

She had meant to leave then. Instead she asked whether the back door still stuck in wet weather, and Petersen said that it did, that he had planed it twice and given up, and they went out through it together to look at the garden, which was not square at all but running to seed in a way her mother would have called honest and her aunt would have called a disgrace. The sea was where it had always been, grey and unbothered, at the end of the field.

"You could come back in the summer," Petersen said, "if you wanted to see it dry."

Ada said she might. On the train home she set the clock on the seat beside her and did not wind it, and was surprised, somewhere past the third station, to find that she was not sorry she had come.
